newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong firms eager to spin off China property.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong firms eager to spin off China property.

text.p: China's improving economy has prompted some Hong Kong-listed firms to spin off first their China infrastructure units and now their China property arms, analysts said.
China's easier credit policy in the second half of 1996 has fuelled hopes of economic recovery and some believe the economic cycle may peak in 1997-98.
"Spinning off property units will definitely become a trend," said Sean He, senior analyst at DBS Securities.
"Companies will try their best to spin off their China property units since they need a lot of money to reinvest back into China," said Kinson Au of PW Asia.
China Resources Enterprise Ltd has already announced its intention to raise between HK$550 million (US$70.5 million) and HK$850 million by seeking a separate listing for its China property unit.
Analysts said the company planned an analysts presentation concerning the listing of China Resources Beijing Land Ltd on October 17.
Chinese Estates Holdings Ltd has applied for a separate listing of its China property projects in Hong Kong.
"It plans to sell the new shares by way of introducing the company to private investors," a securities source said.
Earlier this month, newspapers reported that Pacific Concord Holding Ltd planned to spin off its China and Hong Kong property arm.

Analysts said the success of the new share issues would depend on the location and quality of the companies' land banks and their pricing policies, since property is relatively risky compared to power plants and toll roads.
"The market is still sceptical on China property," said Andrew Kuet at Morgan Grenfell Asia Securities.

Henderson China Holdings Ltd, the China property arm of Henderson Land Development Co Ltd, listed last March on the Hong Kong stock exchange. The stock was issued at HK$21.50 and closed at HK$18.20 on Friday.
However, analysts said China Resource Beijing should be attractive if its shares are priced at a more than 30 percent discount to net asset value since the location of its land bank was good.
"The company is involved in the redevelopment of Beijing's Xidan district," Kuet said. He said its parent, state-owned China Resources, should help the company secure good projects in China.
But companies which have invested in only commercial and residential properties in China's southern province of Guangdong might find difficulties in attracting investors, analysts said.
Guangdong's provincial planning commission deputy director Zhen Guorui said in August that Guangdong had banned new property projects for 12 months to reduce the stockpile of empty flats.
The province is facing a mis-matching problem as a large number of empty housing units are too expensive for Guangdong citizens to buy. (US$1=HK$7.3)
